meta.notes: Primary ICP from context: South Asian diaspora dietitians abroad (US/UK/Canada/Australia). 18 prospects found (target was 20+; one more, a Toronto RD, was dropped because its only fetchable page shares a directory domain with another prospect); several are evidenced only via association/public directories (BDA Find a Dietitian, Dietitians Australia Find an APD, Medimap, Dietitian Central, PCRM) because their own sites were unfetchable or absent; contacts were taken only from the practices' own pages. Time-per-plan figures come mostly from vendors and a coach with affiliate interests; no independent survey found. Reddit, G2, Capterra, Upwork/Fiverr and several journal pages blocked Preuve's fetcher. Indian vendor claims (Nutrena, mealPlan.fit, WellnessZ, Hint) are self-reported. No evidence found on how dietitians decide on software purchases beyond price points.

summary.statement: Reported time per manual meal plan ranges from 30-60 minutes (vendor claim) to 2-3 hours (vendor blog) to 4-6 hours (a coach's own practice).
Dietitians describe plan-building time as a top pain point, even with software.
No independent survey of plan-building time was found; most figures come from vendors.
Dietitians abroad report a gap in understanding South Asian foods, and clients ask for meal plans with regular Indian foods.
Mainstream USDA-based databases and older Indian tables cover regional Indian food poorly.
In India, several vendors already sell large Indian/regional food databases (Nutrena 8,000+ dishes across 28 state cuisines; mealPlan.fit IFCT; Hint), so the gap is mainly in Western tools.
The manual process is recipe research plus typing plans into Word, spreadsheets, and, in India, sending them on WhatsApp.
Some dietitians, including leading South Asian-focused RDNs, deliberately do not make standalone meal plans the main deliverable.
Price points are established: That Clean Life $30-60/mo; abroad, practices pay an add-on on top of Practice Better/Healthie.
Indian competitors price from Rs 499 (Hint, WellnessZ) and Rs 999 (Nutrena) to Rs 2,999 (mealPlan.fit) per month.
No evidence found on who decides or which factors drive the decision beyond price; in solo practices the buyer is presumably the dietitian.
Practice software meal planning (Practice Better, Healthie) is described as weak, which pushes users to add-ons.
The add-on slot is already filled: That Clean Life generates plans from calories/macros/diet type and integrates natively with Practice Better.
Indian tools already generate 7-day plans with AI in seconds to minutes.
Studies show general LLM meal plans underperform dietitians, including for an Indian vegetarian profile, and researchers advise expert-facing use only.
Builders report LLMs invent calorie counts unless constrained to a validated dish list, which supports a curated-database approach.
No direct evidence found of dietitians' stated confidence in existing tools' recipe accuracy.
Allergens and preferences are checked by hand in manual plans, and handled by recipe filters in tools.
Competing AI tools already take food preferences and conditions as inputs.

current_solutions.statement: Many dietitians still build plans by hand in Word or spreadsheets; in India plans go out over WhatsApp.
Abroad, practices pair Practice Better or Healthie with a meal-plan add-on such as That Clean Life, which already auto-generates plans.
In India, Nutrena, mealPlan.fit, WellnessZ and Hint already sell AI or template plan generation on Indian food databases for Rs 499-2,999/month.
Some dietitians avoid prescriptive meal plans and sell counselling instead.
